title: Regular Expressions
summary: Test, extract, replace, and split text with regular expression literals and the string methods that use them.
intro: String methods like `includes` and `split` look for fixed text. A regular expression describes a *shape* of text instead, such as five digits or a word followed by an equals sign, so one short pattern can validate input, pull values out, rewrite text, and split it.

steps.title: Testing patterns
steps.body:
Write a regular expression between slashes, with optional flags after the closing slash, and call `test` to ask whether a string contains that shape. It returns true or false:

```javascript
console.log(/\d{5}/.test("zip 90210")); // true
```

The pieces you will use most:

| Piece | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `\d`, `\w`, `\s` | a digit, a word character (an unaccented letter, a digit, or `_`), a whitespace character |
| `.` | any one character except a line break |
| `[aeiou]`, `[A-Z]`, `[0-9a-f]` | one character from a set or a range |
| `+`, `*`, `?` | one or more, zero or more, optional |
| `{5}`, `{2,9}` | exactly 5, from 2 to 9 |
| `^`, `$` | the start and the end of the string |

A quantifier applies to the piece right before it, so `[A-Z]{2}` means two capital letters.

Without anchors, `test` searches anywhere, so `/\d{5}/.test("123456")` is true. Wrap a validator in `^...$` to check the whole string. The `i` flag ignores case: `/^[a-z]+$/i` accepts `Ada`.

Characters such as `. ( ) [ ] { } ^ $ ? + * /` have special meanings, so put a backslash before one to match it literally: `\.`, `\(`, `\)`, `\$`. Inside a set most of them are literal already, so `[.()]` matches a dot or a parenthesis.

example.title: Form validators
example.prompt: Check zip codes, usernames, and phone numbers against anchored patterns and print whether each one is valid.
example.output:
12345: valid
1234: invalid
12a45: invalid
Ada_99: valid
x1: invalid
9lives: invalid
grace: valid
(555) 123-4567: valid
(555)123-4567: valid
555-123-4567: invalid
example.explanation: Each validator is anchored with `^` and `$`, so the whole string must fit. `\d{5}` wants exactly five digits, which rules out `1234` and `12a45`. A username starts with one letter (`[a-z]` with the `i` flag also accepts `A`), then has 2 to 9 word characters, so it is 3 to 10 long: `x1` is too short and `9lives` starts with a digit. The phone pattern escapes the parentheses with `\(` and `\)`, and `\s?` makes the space optional, so both bracketed forms pass.

practice.title: Store validators
practice.prompt:
Write three validators for product codes, hex colors, and prices.

1. `isProductCode(text)`: two capital letters, a dash, then exactly four digits, such as `AB-1234`.
2. `isHexColor(text)`: a `#` followed by exactly six hex digits (`0` to `9` and `a` to `f`), in any case, such as `#1a2B3c`.
3. `isPrice(text)`: a `$`, one or more digits, a dot, then exactly two digits, such as `$4.99`.
4. Each must check the whole string. The loops at the bottom already print the results.

Expected output:

```text
AB-1234: valid
ab-1234: invalid
ABC-123: invalid
XY-98765: invalid
#1a2B3c: valid
#FFF: invalid
00ff00: invalid
#00FF00: valid
$4.99: valid
$12.50: valid
4.99: invalid
$3.5: invalid
```

tests.output:
AB-1234: valid
ab-1234: invalid
ABC-123: invalid
XY-98765: invalid
#1a2B3c: valid
#FFF: invalid
00ff00: invalid
#00FF00: valid
$4.99: valid
$12.50: valid
4.99: invalid
$3.5: invalid

hints: Start every pattern with `^` and end it with `$` so the whole string must match.
Use the `i` flag for the hex color so `[0-9a-f]` also accepts capital letters.
In the price, `$` and `.` are special, so write them as `\$` and `\.`.

steps.title: Finding matches

example.title: Numbers and settings
example.prompt: Sum every number in a sentence, read the first key=value pair with numbered groups, then list every pair with named groups.
example.output:
Numbers: 3, 12, 7
Total: 22
Numbers in plain text: 0
First pair: host=local
Key: host, value: local
host -> local
port -> 8080
debug -> true
example.explanation: `/\d+/g` finds every run of digits, and `reduce` converts each string with `Number` while summing. Text with no digits gives `null`, and `?? []` turns that into an empty array, so `.length` is safe. Without `g`, `match` stops at `host=local` and returns its groups: index 0 is the whole match, 1 and 2 are the parentheses. `matchAll` then walks all three pairs, and the named groups make the print line read like the data.

practice.title: Hashtags and dates
practice.prompt:
Pull hashtags out of a post and dates out of a log line.

1. Collect every hashtag in `post` with `match` and `/#\w+/g`, then print `Tags: ` with them joined by `, ` and `Count: ` with how many there are.
2. Do the same search on `quiet`, defaulting with `?? []`, and print `Tags in quiet post: ` with the count.
3. Use `match` without `g` and three numbered groups to find the first date in `log`. Print `First date: ` with the whole match, then `Year: <year>, month: <month>` filled from groups 1 and 2.
4. Loop over `log.matchAll` with named groups `year` and `month` and print each date as `year/month`, in the order they appear.

Expected output:

```text
Tags: #javascript, #regex, #100DaysOfCode
Count: 3
Tags in quiet post: 0
First date: 2024-03-15
Year: 2024, month: 03
2024/03
2024/04
2024/11
```

tests.output:
Tags: #javascript, #regex, #100DaysOfCode
Count: 3
Tags in quiet post: 0
First date: 2024-03-15
Year: 2024, month: 03
2024/03
2024/04
2024/11

hints: `match` with a `g` regex gives `null` when nothing matches, so add `?? []` before you read `.length`.
A date is four digits, a dash, two digits, a dash, and two digits. Wrap each part in parentheses so index 1 holds the year and index 2 the month.
For `matchAll`, add the `g` flag, name the parts with `(?<year>...)` and `(?<month>...)`, and read `match.groups.year`.

steps.title: Replacing and splitting
steps.body:
With a plain string or a regex without `g`, `replace` changes only the first match. Give it a regex with the `g` flag and it changes every match. `replaceAll` takes a regex too, but only a `g` one: without the flag it throws a TypeError.

```javascript
console.log("a  b   c".replace(/\s+/g, " ")); // a b c
```

In the replacement string, `$1` and `$2` insert numbered groups and `$<name>` inserts a named group:

```javascript
console.log("2024-01-15".replace(/(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})/, "$3/$2/$1")); // 15/01/2024
console.log("port=8080".replace(/(?<key>\w+)=(?<value>\w+)/, "$<key>: $<value>")); // port: 8080
```

When the new text has to be computed, pass a function instead. It receives the whole match, then each group, and returns the replacement. Name a parameter you skip `_`:

```javascript
const doubleDigit = (_, letter, digit) => `${letter}${Number(digit) * 2}`;
console.log("x3 y5".replace(/(\w)(\d)/g, doubleDigit)); // x6 y10
```

`split` accepts a regex as well. `split(/\s+/)` splits on any run of whitespace, and `split(/\s*[,;]\s*/)` splits on a comma or semicolon with optional spaces around it. Trim first, or a leading space gives an empty first item.

> Gotcha: a `g` regex remembers where its last match ended in `lastIndex`, and `test` starts from there next time. Leave `g` off a regex you use with `test`.

```javascript
const re = /cat/g;
console.log(`${re.test("cat")} ${re.test("cat")}`); // true false
```

example.title: Text cleanup
example.prompt: Collapse extra spaces, double the counts in an order, reorder dates, and split a messy list.
example.output:
too many spaces
6 apples and 24 pears
from 15/01/2024 to 01/02/2024
4 items: a | b | c | d
example.explanation: `replaceAll` with `/\s+/g` turns each run of spaces into one space. The replacer in `doubleCounts` skips the whole match with `_`, gets the count and the item from the two groups, and rebuilds the text with the count doubled. `$3/$2/$1` reorders the date groups, and `g` converts both dates. The split pattern eats a comma or semicolon plus any spaces around it, so every item comes out clean.

practice.title: Chat cleanup
practice.prompt:
Fix up chat messages, names, and spacing with regex replace and split.

1. `replaceSmileys(text)`: turn every `:)` into `😊` and every `:(` into `😞`, using one regex with a group for the mouth and a replacer function `(_, mouth) => ...`.
2. `toFirstLast(fullName)`: turn `Lovelace, Ada` into `Ada Lovelace` with `$2 $1` in the replacement.
3. `splitWords(text)`: split on any run of whitespace and return the array.
4. The bottom of the file already prints the results.

Expected output:

```text
Nice work 😊 but the build broke 😞 fix it 😊
Ada Lovelace
3 words: one | two | three
```

tests.output:
Nice work 😊 but the build broke 😞 fix it 😊
Ada Lovelace
3 words: one | two | three

hints: Inside a set the parentheses are literal, so `[()]` matches either mouth. Put that set in a group right after the colon so the replacer receives it.
The replacer returns `"😊"` when `mouth === ")"` and `"😞"` otherwise.
For the name, capture the word before the comma and the word after the comma and space, then use `"$2 $1"` as the replacement.

recap:
- `/pattern/flags` is a regex literal, and `regex.test(str)` returns true or false.
- `\d`, `\w`, `\s`, and `.` match one character of a kind. `[aeiou]` and `[A-Z]` match one from a set or range.
- `+`, `*`, `?`, `{n}`, and `{n,m}` repeat the piece before them.
- `^` and `$` anchor a validator to the whole string. The `i` flag ignores case.
- Escape special characters with a backslash: `\.`, `\(`, `\)`, `\$`.
- `str.match(/.../g) ?? []` gives every match. Without `g`, `match` gives the first match with its groups, or `null`.
- `( )` captures a group read as `m[1]`, and `(?<name>...)` is read as `m.groups.name`.
- `str.matchAll(/.../g)` loops over every match with its groups.
- `replace` with a `g` regex changes every match, and `replaceAll` requires `g`.
- `$1` and `$<name>` insert groups, and a replacer function `(match, group1) => ...` computes each replacement.
- `split(/\s+/)` and `split(/\s*[,;]\s*/)` split on flexible separators.
- A `g` regex remembers `lastIndex`, so leave `g` off regexes used with `test`.
